speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Thirty years later, more than half of the global population, or 4.4 billion, are active Internet users, 3.5 billion of whom are on social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The ubiquity of technology, the way it is embedded in every aspect of our everyday lives, is a given.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It has gone beyond just being a useful tool to help us perform tasks to becoming the primary means by which we search for information, communicate and socialise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is commonplace to see families, groups of friends, all sitting around a table, all looking down at their phones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singaporeans are at the vanguard of growth in Internet use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2017, Singapore, alongside Sweden, topped the Global Inclusive Internet Index.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This index measures the adoption and ease of access to the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There is no question about the benefits of the Internet and social media and the convenience that they bring to our lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: But these benefits also come at a price.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In exchange for this convenience, we have, in turn, bestowed significant power on the social media companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We voluntarily surrender personal data to them, exposing the most intimate details of our lives on social media websites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are often unaware that websites and companies are collecting and amassing our data, without our knowledge, until perhaps a scandal breaks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: After the first discovery, that mistake was hidden from the public for over half a year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Amazon's Alexa, as another example, an "always on" device in our homes – Bloomberg recently revealed that the team charged with auditing commands given to Alexa had access to customers’ home addresses and other personal information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Alexa also recorded private conversation and sent it to a user’s acquaintance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In short, there is no adequate way to moderate and control how this information is used or shared by others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And it is not a simple matter of a leak of data or loss of privacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Many of us think that we still have some measure of control over our privacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some brush off loss of privacy, saying it is a worthwhile exchange for the convenience and benefits that technology brings to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: But we fail to recognise that the digital traces that we leave online can be connected and thereafter shared with others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are wide-reaching and sometimes devastating repercussions that could occur.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are some key areas of concern for us and I will enumerate them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Cyberbullying is, really, traditional playground bullying transmuted into an online new digital form.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In many ways, it is more insidious than traditional bullying.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There is anonymity, and there is a lack of a physical confrontation and it allows people to engage in conduct that they may not ordinarily engage in, in normal daily life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The abusive comments that are put up can be permanently displayed on the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They are broadcast to a large online community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And in truth, the victim has nowhere to hide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In our 2014 Second Reading speech on the Protection from Harassment Bill, the Government highlighted alarming trends about cyberbullying.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Since then, matters have grown worse and I will cite a few numbers to this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In a 2019 Google survey, teachers in Singapore view the need to prevent cyberbullying as the most pressing concern when it comes to teaching children about online safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The latest research suggests that bullying may cause physical changes in the brain, increasing the risk of mental illness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Studies have also shown that bullying in childhood has effects that last into adulthood as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Mental problems, including anxiety, depression, suicidal tendencies, poor general health, lower educational, financial and social functioning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Many suffer in silence and we may not know until it is too late.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In Singapore, for instance, it was reported a few years ago that a 13-year-old girl was bullied by her friends on Facebook and in a WhatsApp group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She started cutting herself with metal rulers and razor blades as a result, causing injury to herself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the United States (US), a 12-year-old girl in Florida hung herself after being subjected to cyberbullying by two 12-year-olds: rumours about having sexually transmitted diseases, vulgar name-calling and the like.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), a 17-year-old boy in Manchester stepped in front of a train after he was called a "black rat" and "ugly" online, both by people he knew and also by people who were complete strangers to him.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The second area of concern is in doxxing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Doxxing is the disclosure of personal information to cause violence or harassment to others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The term was originally used in 1990s to describe a tactic used by hackers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They would release dossiers of personal information about other hackers, to breach their anonymity and expose them to harassment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are familiar with some local examples, such as in the Caltex incident, Members would know about the couple who pushed the old man at Toa Payoh hawker centre; and, of course, the Anton Casey case, where he had to leave Singapore as a result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some may say that these people get what they deserve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It has been used as a political tool by extremists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Can you imagine if you were one of these 1,400?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In New Zealand, in the wake of the Christchurch terror attacks, an anti-gun control Facebook group posted contact details of the Queenstown detective online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One post featured an image of a rifle and words, "Come and take it".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: You can imagine how dangerous this information is, and can be, in the hands of the wrong people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Also in New York, a journalist, Asher Wolf, made anti-war posts online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Her address was shared on the dark web, and people posted dog faeces through to her, in her mailbox.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In South Africa, a journalist, Karima Brown, her contact details were published on Twitter by the leader of the Economic Freedom Fighters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She received an onslaught of graphic messages threatening rape and murder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some threatened to expose her flesh by peeling her skin off.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: After the Boston Marathon bombings, online citizens on Reddit wrongly identified Sunil Tripathi as the Boston bomber.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The family received hundreds of threatening and anti-Islamic messages, even though they are not Muslim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Falsehoods are disseminated even more easily today for a number of reasons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They have shorter attention spans, people skim, rather than critically evaluate content.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They tend to share information because it triggers an emotional response more so than because of its credibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Users generally share links without even having read them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When content gets shared enough times, it seems and appears more credible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There is also a market for online disinformation tools and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Fake social media accounts are commonly used to spread falsehoods. "Click farms" consisting of large numbers of low-paid workers can be used to sell video views, "likes" and even votes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Bots can sometimes take the place of these low-cost workers as well in enhancing the spread of this online disinformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Other online influencers can also be paid to spread false content, and clickbaits can be used to profit from Internet traffic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Falsehoods affect people, real people in real life, as well as entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some examples: it affects those close to home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One of our local actresses: messages were circulated suggesting that she had a sexually transmitted disease (STD).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She started receiving messages such as: "Are you a prostitute?" and "Heard you have STD.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Get well soon." Lewd comments continued to surface even after the facts were put out and it affected her reputation even when she tried to venture overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Recently, the Select Committee on Online Falsehoods heard from a new citizen, Mr Hetamsaria, falsely identified in an article as a new citizen who was disappointed with Singapore and considering giving up his citizenship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The family was deeply affected by numerous xenophobic comments made about them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Just last week, there was fake news on Facebook that a veteran of our local acting scene, Lim Kay Tong, received a 16-year sentence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When users clicked on the link, it led to a recipe for tikka, and another linked to a recipe for pumpkin spice cheesecake.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: But the impact of the clickbait was self-evident.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There was also fake news circulating on WhatsApp claiming that Fandi Ahmad was taken into custody for hurting someone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Falsehoods about companies can cause them irreversible damage, set off a public relations nightmare and cause economic damage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There have been stories claiming that clear, parasite worms were found in bottles of Dasani across the country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Several hundred people had been sent to hospital as a result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had shut down a manufacturing plant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Coca-Cola, of course, denied this, as did FDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) FairPrice, closer to home, was affected by multiple rumours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2007, a photo suggesting NTUC sold halal pork circulated on the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similar rumours later affected Ya Kun Kaya Toast and a Yong Tau Foo business at Westgate shopping mall.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2017, Members would recall that there was a post going around social media suggesting that FairPrice's house brand rice was made of plastic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Studies paint a bleak picture of a world where the spread of falsehoods over social media is quick, wide and pervasive, whilst truth, even if it corrects the original falsehood, lags far behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A Massachusetts Institute of Technology study analysed 126,000 rumours that spread on Twitter over 12 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Another study by the Journal of Experimental Psychology indicated that repeated exposure to a false statement on social media made it more believable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And, finally, in a University of Buffalo study, 20,000 tweets during Hurricane Sandy and the Boston Marathon bombing showed that 86% to 91% of active twitter users spread falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Nearly as many did nothing to correct that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is self-evident, partly from what I have seen and partly I am sure from Members' own experience, that the Internet is almost impossible to control, akin to a lawless jungle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As in any jungle, the weakest and most vulnerable are disproportionately affected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Recent surveys showed multiracial females have the highest risk of being harassed online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Adolescent girls are more likely to experience cyberbullying than boys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Seventy-five percent of children with autism are bullied online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Seventy percent of children with physical defects are bullied online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) teens are five times more at risk of being abused on Facebook than non-LGBT teens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This online harassment translates into real world violence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One in three women in the US experiences domestic violence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Nearly 90% of domestic abuse shelters and programmes report that abusers have intimidated and made threats against them using electronic means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: An Australian survey found that 98% of domestic violence practitioners reported clients who experienced technology-facilitated abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We cannot trust the Internet companies to regulate this jungle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Because their primary motivation is the pursuit of profit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In an internal company memo, Facebook Vice President Andrew Bosworth in June 2016 claimed that any growth, any growth on Facebook was good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Maybe someone dies in a terrorist attack coordinated on our tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The ugly truth is that we believe in connecting people so deeply that anything that allows us to connect more people more often is de facto good." This memo leaked two weeks after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There is not enough transparency in how administrative standards are derived and enforced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are no democratic process and no court process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Facebook only made public its community standards in 2018 after the Cambridge Analytica scandal erupted, 14 years after Facebook was first founded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: People have no faith in social media giants to contain harassment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Users have complained that social media companies have taken days to address their complaints about harassment, if at all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A poll in the UK this year showed that more than half the reports that women lodge about harassment on Facebook are met with either no response or response that the behaviour did not breach their own community guidelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A Singaporean girl saw a Minister to complain that she had her picture put up on Facebook by a male acquaintance, along with derogatory remarks containing sexual innuendo.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She wrote to Facebook, whose response was, that it did not violate their community standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Last year, a US Democratic strategist received threatening tweets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: He complained to Twitter, which said it did not violate rules against abusive behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The man later sent pipe bombs to politicians, and then, at that stage, Twitter said its earlier assessment was wrong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The actress who accused James Franco of sexual misconduct was also repeatedly harassed on Instagram.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She made a report to the Federal Bureau of Investigation and said that Instagram ignored almost all her complaints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Tech companies have admitted that they are unable to deal with some of these problems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, first, let me take Members back to our first attempt in 2014 to deal with online harassment holistically, when this piece of legislation was first enacted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This, as Members will recall, was the first piece of legislation dedicated to protecting victims of harassment, both offline and online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It laid down clear norms as to what constitutes unacceptable social behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The presence of this framework encouraged victims to come forward to seek help, to seek redress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These numbers demonstrate how important POHA has been as an avenue of relief to victims of harassment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In introducing the revisions today, we have taken keen interest in feedback on POHA from at least three groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And finally, from the victims of harassment themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the process of obtaining relief under this Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is clear to us that processes under POHA can be simplified further, made cheaper and also faster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The current process of applying for an expedited protection order (EPO) and protection order (PO) can be streamlined.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some victims have said, they feel that they need the assistance of a lawyer to navigate the current process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In contrast, there is a simpler and more inexpensive method to apply for a personal protection order (PPO) under the Women’s Charter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Those victims who choose instead to file a Magistrate’s Complaint face some difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the outcome of the complaint often turns on the conclusion of Police investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Victims do not know when these investigations might conclude.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A victim who has filed a complaint with the Magistrate, does not have the benefit of the protections afforded by a PO.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If a PO is necessary, the victim has to separately apply for one in the civil Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We can simplify the procedure, so that a victim does not have to provide evidence of his or her harassment more than once.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We can also ensure that we prevent the duplication because reliving the experience only causes further mental anguish for the victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, feedback received is that the Courts should also be given more powers when making orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In particular, the scope of the POs should be widened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It should cover related persons of the victim, as harassers often target persons close to the victim in order to get to the victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Courts should be able to order offenders to be sent for psychiatric assessment and treatments where appropriate as there are cases where mental illnesses may well be the root of the offender’s behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, it was suggested that POs should also be given more bite.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This perceived lack of severity might be another factor which deters victims from coming forward and applying for POs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Further, our attention was also drawn to a specific group of victims, namely, victims of intimate partner violence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These are often victims in a romantic relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If unmarried, they do not qualify for protection under the Women’s Charter, which only protects victims of family violence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some might assume that it might be easier for an unmarried victim to break off the abusive relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the psyche of an abused partner is sometimes the same, whether married or unmarried.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The intimacy of the relationship allows the abuser to create a psychological hold over the victim and makes it difficult for the victim to break free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Research shows that romantic love can sometimes be like an addiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Of these, two-thirds had their first abusive relationship in their teens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On average, for 20% of those who were abused by their spouses or were themselves abusers, the abuse started when they were first dating.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She dated a man for five years, they had five children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Dating violence started in the first year of their relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The man began by shouting vulgarities at her.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It escalated to physical violence when he hit, kicked, slammed her face on the floor, threatened her with a knife.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And all of this, in front of the children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: He threatened to kill himself or the children and abused the children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: He would follow Mdm A everywhere and track her whereabouts via calls, texts, global positioning system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When Mdm A decided to seek help, she could not apply for a PPO under the Women's Charter as she was unmarried.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Her first child who did not carry the man’s name on her birth certificate was in the same position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She could only apply for PPOs for the other four children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are other such cases, and I am sure Members themselves will be familiar with their own experiences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We need to find a way for people in intimate relationships, who are the subject of serious abuse, to get POs more easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: PAVE, in particular, highlighted this strongly to us and has advised the Government on how best to deal with the situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As a result, we amended the Penal Code yesterday and are proposing amendments to POHA today to further strengthen the recourse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We have carefully considered the feedback, some of which I have sketched out, from stakeholders alongside the need for greater regulation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will improve the process of obtaining relief from the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PHC will be dedicated to dealing with harassment matters, whether online or offline, and will have oversight of all criminal and civil cases under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It will be sited in the State Courts and will have the jurisdiction of a District Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The judges will be specially trained to deal with harassment matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Volunteers will be on hand to help victims navigate the Court process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In egregious cases, it may not suffice to grant the victim a civil remedy in the form of a PO.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The law may need to deal with the offender even if the victim has not already gone to the Police.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, the Court has a proactive duty to look at facts, circumstances in the course of granting the EPO.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If it is, the judge must refer the matter to the Police.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The intention is for serious cases of hurt or harassment which come to the Court to be referred to the Police.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will ensure that the state can intervene and intervene at an early stage to reduce the risk of further or greater hurt to the victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, we are taking measures to help victims to meet the burden of proof.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In other words, the victim will not have to prove his or her case more than once.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In terms of streamlining procedures and expediting timelines, we have worked with the State Courts to do so, so that the process for applying for a PO under POHA will, as far as possible, be aligned to that under the Women's Charter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The victim will be able to file an application for a PO using a simplified form at the PHC or online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Relief will also be quicker and more permanent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The victim will no longer have to renew the EPOs every 28 days.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The hearings will also be conducted more quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The PHC will aim to conduct hearings for final POs within four weeks of the application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The timelines, of course, will be subject to practical constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, if an application is filed over the weekend, the Courts may only be able to hear it on the next working day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Applicants should, of course, always seek Police intervention if they are in immediate physical danger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, in that situation, an EPO will be in place until the PO is granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We hope that these measures will relieve some of the anxieties that an applicant faces when invoking the Court process and encourage those in need to come forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, in terms of enhancing the protection for harassment victims and related persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will enhance the protection for these categories of persons, expand the scope of POs and the powers available to the Court when granting a PO.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, clause 16(1) widens the ambit of POs to deal specifically with the situation where an offender may publish a harassing communication which is then shared by others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A PO can now be made to prevent the publication of communications which are not just identical but also substantially similar to the offending communication.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, clause 16(2) clarifies that Internet intermediaries can be ordered to disable access to an offending communication published on their platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is to try to clamp down on harassing communications going viral or spreading even further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, clause 16(2) extends the scope of POs to protect related persons of the victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will ensure that individuals such as Mdm A, in my example, will be able to obtain POs for herself and her children, rather than have to live with the abuse and to worry about potential harassment or abuse to her children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, we have acted on feedback that the Courts should be empowered to proactively intervene in cases where the harasser’s conduct may not cross the threshold of criminal or dangerous conduct, but where the facts demonstrate that the harasser is mentally ill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And the criteria are that (a) the respondent must have a psychiatric condition susceptible to treatment, capable of being treated; (b) the respondent must be suitable for treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The psychiatric condition must have contributed to the contravention that formed the basis for making a PO, having a nexus with the conduct complained of.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The criteria and nature of the treatment will largely mirror the treatment regime under the Criminal Procedure Code, with appropriate safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Failure to comply with the orders will be punishable as contempt of Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Two further amendments in clause 16(1)(a) clarify the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: POs can be obtained against entities who commit contraventions under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The common law principles of attribution will apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will address cases that have already been brought before our Courts, for example, where wayward companies might have crossed the threshold of lawful debt collection into criminal behavior, such as intentional harassment or violence, in the context of conducting their lawful activity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, harassing, intentional harassing, sometimes violence, in the context of carrying out their debt collection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Companies may have sent different runners to harass a victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Victims can now obtain a single PO against the company and they do not have to bring each runner who conducts each of these harassing acts to Court each time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Domestic exclusion orders are available under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These orders, which are also available under the Women’s Charter, will allow victims to exclude a harasser from their shared residence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is so even if the harasser has a proprietary interest in the residence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are also taking measures to strengthen the recourse available to victims and increase the deterrence factor of the remedies available under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, clauses 4 to 10 and 13 clarify that entities can be liable for contraventions under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They can be prosecuted or sued for damages, and the common law principles of attribution will apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will discourage entities from allowing their employees to harass customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, this House heard yesterday about amendments to the Penal Code to double penalties for offences committed against vulnerable persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, we spoke earlier about the pressing need to protect victims of intimate partner violence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Government has amended the Penal Code to provide for enhanced penalties for specific offences committed against intimate partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are also taking steps to ensure that a harasser who re-offends is also dealt with severely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, as I mentioned earlier, breach of a PO under POHA is not an arrestable offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in contrast with the position under the Women’s Charter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In response to concerns that POs issued under the Act are perceived as ineffective, we propose to amend the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This also brings the Act in line with the Women’s Charter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I spoke earlier about the scourge of technology when not handled properly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To understand the basis of the doxxing amendments, let me first highlight a case that might fall through the cracks today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A Singaporean girl, whom I shall not name, was in the middle of her GCE "O" level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She discovered edited photographs of herself on a Tumblr blog with pornographic content.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: She started receiving unsolicited messages on her social media platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One day, she noticed a man following her home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Her former best friend, it turned out, had emailed her full name, photos, address and names of the school and tuition centres that she attended to over 60 porn blogs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With this knowledge, she retreated from her social interactions, afraid to even leave her home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This young girl was a victim of harassment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the email sent by her friend to the porn blogs, despite its malicious intent, may not have been caught by existing POHA provisions which require communications to be "threatening, abusive or insulting" in themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The doxxing amendments are an extension of the existing provisions on harassment and seek to deal with this lacuna in the law today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For this offence, the intention or knowledge of the publisher is key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Doxxing will be made out if the person published identity information of another person: intending to cause harassment, alarm or distress; intending to cause the victim to fear that unlawful violence will be used against him or another person, or to facilitate unlawful violence against the victim; or knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the publication is likely to cause the victim to fear that unlawful violence will be used against him or another person, or to facilitate unlawful violence against the victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Identity information is defined as information that on its own or with other information identifies, or purports to identify, the victim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes photographs, contact details, address and place of employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new offence will not affect most people, who continue to engage constructively on the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It does not stop them from: identifying the perpetrators of crimes, including traffic offences or POHA offences or, indeed from posting videos of public disputes to give a factual account of an incident.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On the other hand, publishing someone’s contact details to netizens intending to harass or alarm that person or intending that other netizens use the information to harass or hurt the person, is unacceptable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Publishing photographs and contact details of a girl, intending that others use those details to harass her, is likewise unacceptable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There have been concerns raised that the new doxxing provisions could be too broad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These similar concerns were raised about the existing harassment provisions back in 2014.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Harassment is heavily fact-specific, and doxxing is a subset of that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The law today, in fact, with these amendments, adds clarity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Doxxing is currently prosecuted through a mix of provisions arising in different pieces of legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Courts will now be able to develop a body of jurisprudence on when the offence is made out and, furthermore, existing case law on when intent is made out in the circumstances can be relied upon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Other concerns have also been raised about whether the new provisions can deal with anonymous posters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Anonymity is not a new issue under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Minister Shanmugam, when he spoke on this Bill in 2014, addressed this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Even if the respondent or publisher is anonymous, he may be identified by an Internet location address, website or other unique identifier as the Court may order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition, POs are binding, even if the person behind the account may not be identified.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The POs can be served on multiple accounts as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As with the other victims of harassment, such as cyberbullying and intimate partner violence, a victim of doxxing will be able to avail himself of the streamlined processes and expedited timelines as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The falsehoods regime under POHA aims to help individuals to give recourse and redress against the effects of falsehoods whilst, at the same time, striking the balance with the right of people to hold their own opinions and debate matters of interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Broadly, POHA categorises the remedies available by types of orders which are available, split into five categories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Section 15 deals with the final orders which can be given in cases of falsehoods, and section 16 deals, amongst others, with interim orders for the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is similar to the approach taken in section 12, which makes a PO available against both persons, entities and Internet intermediaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In contrast, the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Bill has distinct parts dealing with individuals versus corporate entities, and these are found in Part III and Part IV of that Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes misleading statements but does not cover criticisms, opinions, satire or parody.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, a statement that omits material facts is misleading if the statement would have been considered by a reasonable person to be misleading by reason of such omission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If, for example, A says that B is dishonest, that is a statement of opinion and not a false statement of fact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, if A goes on to say that B was convicted by a Court of cheating, then this is a false statement of fact if B was never convicted of such an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is also false if B was subsequently acquitted on appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The statement is also false if B was subsequently acquitted on appeal, because the statement conveys a false meaning by reason of its omission of B’s subsequent acquittal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was necessary, given the speed at which online falsehoods can now spread.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the case of interim disabling orders and targeted interim notification orders, which are directed at Internet intermediaries, notice of the application first has to be served on the Internet intermediary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is because the Internet intermediary is not directly responsible for the falsehood, and should be given a chance to explain its position in Court, should it wish to contest the application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As is the case under the current Act, the Court will not make any of these orders unless satisfied, amongst other things, that, one, the statement being complained of is false; and two, it is just and equitable in the circumstances to make the order being sought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The test of when it is just and equitable to grant a section 15 order has been set out by our Courts in case law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a flexible one, taking into account various factors, including but not limited to the nature of the false statement; the seriousness of the allegation made; the degree to which the statement has been publicised; whether the subject of the false statement has the means to publicise his or her own version of the truth.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A stop publication order requires a person or entity not to publish a false statement or any substantially similar statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is already available today as I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ensures that publishers cannot game the system by simply amending the statement slightly, but such that it is still false.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As with the present regime, stop publication orders can be taken out against multiple individuals or entities and the applicant need not take out separate applications against multiple persons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Anyone who publishes the false statement or a substantially similar statement is bound upon service unless the Court has dispensed with service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This deals with the situation where an anonymous user may use different online accounts to publish the same false statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will be covered by the order, regardless of which account is used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are available today but fleshed out in the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I spoke earlier about how falsehoods travel faster, deeper and more broadly than truth; and that repeated exposure to false statements on social media make them more believable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There may be cases where it is not enough to order a respondent to stop publishing a falsehood, and it may be necessary to go beyond that to require the respondent person or entity to put the truth out there.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The respondent in such a case will be required to publish a notice online or in a printed publication, stating that the statement in question has been found to be false, and correcting the false statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The respondent will also be required to make the notice available to persons, or specified description of persons, as determined by the Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, on disabling orders which are available today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They can be made to require an Internet intermediary to disable access to a material containing a false statement on the Internet intermediary's platform, so that it is no longer available to viewers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, targeted correction orders which are also available today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are in like vein to correction orders but can be made against an Internet intermediary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It requires an Internet intermediary to distribute a correction of the false statement to viewers of a false statement on the Internet intermediary's platform.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it carries the corrections on the platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Unlike the other orders, they operate against a prescribed third party who has not been responsible for the publication of the false statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This third party, as an example, could be a news outlet, broadcaster or Internet intermediary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The prescribed third party can be required to publish a notice stating that the statement in question has been found to be false, as well as a correction of that false statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Well, the ubiquity of technology nowadays means that falsehoods may spread across several different platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may start on one; it may carry through to one or several others.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It might be difficult to identify who has been exposed to a falsehood.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mainstream purveyors of information, prescribed third parties have a sufficiently wide reach to help to correct viral falsehoods which are particularly serious or persistent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As this order imposes obligations on third parties, interim relief will not be available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of the relevant procedure for these orders, the same streamlined process I mentioned and also, expedited timelines, will apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The interim order will remain in place until it expires or has been cancelled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For those who want to appeal against an order under section 15, they will still need to seek leave under section 21 of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As with the other remedies under POHA, the Government will not have recourse under section 15.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government will have to rely on the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), which is currently still a Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, section 15 orders can be made against both individual persons and corporate entities, but not the Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill builds upon an existing ecosystem to deal with harassment, and to offer victims recourse and redress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is equally integral to this ecosystem that there are the many volunteers, psychiatric institutions, the Police, the news agencies, schools and many others.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are all part of the ecosystem, and we are grateful for their efforts in highlighting harassment issues and broadcasting the remedies available and also assisting with the victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the end of the day, harassment is a social problem which requires a concerted social response.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We all bear a responsibility for ensuring that harassment is not perpetrated or escalated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the surest way to provide victims with protection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We should not tolerate any harassment or violence, least of all, those which occur in an intimate partner or family setting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The legal protection from harassment is as relevant today as when POHA was first enacted in 2014.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cyberbullying is one of the social ills that POHA has sought to address.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides amendments to the criminal law addressing voyeurism, revenge porn and cyber flashing, a PO under POHA is capable of ordering published images that cause harassment, alarm or distress to be taken down.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are several commendable features of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, clause 22 makes contravening a PO an arrestable offence in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This should be welcomed as it would allow for a prompter response, especially when someone is at risk of getting hurt.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Social media can proliferate information that can be used to harass.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether it be through pictures in school uniform, consistent patterns of posts, family pictures, pictures taken near a person’s home, the point is that there is a lot of information online that can be pieced together at strategic times to harass a person, and his or her family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, online words can spark offline consequences and things can spiral out of control.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, the amendments we are debating today in POHA are crucial and timely.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in China, because a person’s car plate number was a partial match to a car belonging to a driver who had spat on a homeless elderly, the "human flesh search engine" caused a person who had consistently protested his innocence to receive blackmail calls, threatening to burn his house down.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: People who speak up about something controversial also get doxxed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Threats to safety, threats to family members, harassment at work, these are all possible consequences of doxxing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, the Bill broadens the kinds of orders that can be made, particularly with respect to false information.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, instead of requiring a person to stop publishing it unless he or she also publishes a notification drawing attention to the falsehood and what is true, a correction order, stop publication order, disabling order, targeted correction order, and general correction order may be ordered under clause 20.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What would be especially useful are interim orders as the falsehoods may be spreading quickly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some of these orders, there are additional criteria which need to be fulfilled beyond the just and equitable basis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, in the new section 15E, a general correction order requires that the publication of the false statement of fact must have caused or is likely to cause serious harm to the reputation of the subject.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For an interim disabling order in the new section 16AA, the additional requirement is that it has caused or is likely to cause the subject harm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I seek a clarification of the Senior Minister of State: is the harm in this section limited to physical harm, or would it extend to other forms of harm?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would point out that there is a specialised definition of harm only for the new section 8A in clause 10(e) which is "any physical harm; harassment, alarm or distress; or being caused to believe that unlawful violence will be used against the victim." On the topic of general correction orders which I have raised above, the Bill will allow general correction orders to be made against third parties, such as Internet intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it could be envisioned that expenses can be incurred by such third parties in complying with and adhering to such orders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus, my question is: does the Bill ensure that such third parties are not put out of the pocket for trying to comply with these orders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The fifth point, Sir, is more of a clarification than a position.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is to be noted that the current section 15 already has the phrase "statement of fact".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This section will be repealed in clause 20.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is the meaning of "statement of fact" in clause 3 meant to be different from how "statement of fact" is to be understood in the current section 15?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sixthly, this Bill makes the overall process quicker and more accessible, primarily by setting up the Protection from Harassment Court (PHC), governed by its own rules of procedure and evidence per clause 24(h).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are several features of the Bill which make it easier for litigants in person.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the proposed section 13B mandates that the Court explain to the respondent in ordinary language the purpose and effect of a mandatory treatment order, consequences if the respondent fails to comply.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond these useful initiatives, are there any other measures in place to ensure that victims of harassment and abuse are given sufficient assistance when they approach the Courts for help?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak on five general matters where I seek clarifications about the application of certain clauses in practice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will also highlight one important area where I feel the Bill falls short in my view.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are shamed, often through social media, with videos of their actions shared and distributed widely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This, in and of itself, is not the issue and the public must be clear that posting and sharing such examples of behaviour is not circumscribed by the Bill, even if other company-specific regulations or codes of conduct apply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, for example, if an individual says that he had to wash the stench of Singapore Mass Rapid Transit or Singapore Bus Services commuters off his body because he had to take public transport for two weeks that his Mercedes Benz or Bentley was in the workshop and he is then pilloried online for such crass remarks, that, in itself, would not be caught by the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What happens, however, in such cases is that the public approbation that ensues has the potential of inviting vigilante justice against the perpetrator and a real risk of personal harm when the private information of the perpetrator is revealed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In some cases, netizens would release identity information, such as the perpetrator's place of work and contact numbers and other personal information, ostensibly in the pursuit of a sense of justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Others, however, may release the information with malicious intent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, there may be a case where an individual's identity information is already online and another online commentator posts a hyperlink to it with an innocuous comment like, "This person is a lawyer and yet he behaves in such a way" – the actively revealed information being uncontroversial – in this case, the occupation of the individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the hyperlink reveals other personal information like place of work and contact numbers, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a case, it would be arguable whether the comment and hyperlink together meet the threshold of intent as required under clause 4 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What would be the Minister's view on such a scenario?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the individual who made the comment, and including the hyperlink, be guilty of an offence in such a case?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second issue could be doxxing carried out by anonymous users on popular third party Facebook pages, something which requires active moderation to combat, a resource most social media sites and Facebook page moderators may not have any real bandwidth to undertake.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would such sites be found liable for the offence of doxxing where there is no intent on the part of the moderators of the page to harass, but because of the ecology and anonymity provided by the Internet, doxxing ensues nonetheless?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I read the Minister for Law's speech at PAVE's Dating Violence Awareness Week Event at *SCAPE in February and the stories shared on IPV and, separately, how PAVE's activism and engagement directly resulted in the amendments in this Bill to address current gaps in the law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), the overwhelming global burden of global IPV is borne by women.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, according to WHO, IPVs also occur in same-sex marriages as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the boundaries of the definition of "misleading" under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill targets both a false statement and a misleading one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While there exists an objective legal test for determining whether a statement of fact is false, can the Minister confirm how the Government expects the Courts to interpret the boundaries of a statement that is misleading in the context of the new remedies provided for under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand from the Minister's Second Reading speech that a reference to the omission of material facts would make out what "misleading" is.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this may not be without controversy, and I will try and use a hypothetical example to explain this point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An individual has made a statement against a black metal band two weeks before it is due to perform, encouraging others not to attend the performance, leading to a loss of revenue and poor ticket sales that can be attributed to the onset of a viral online campaign by an individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The statement released by the individual that is headlined in bold goes like this: "People who listen to black metal music may commit violence in the real world", alongside pictures of individuals with heavily tattooed faces.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the standpoint of the black metal band, whose music may undoubtedly not be everyone's cup of tea, the statement is misleading because all sorts of people may commit violence in the real world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, a statement can potentially be misleading if it does not cover all the relevant facts or represent the matter fairly, and the choice of which facts are chosen usually turns on where you stand on any given matter, philosophically, politically or morally, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this scenario, what remedies will be available to the band under the new clause 20(1) of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand there is a corpus of literature on misleading statements when it comes to securities law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be helpful if the Minister could share with the House and lay members of the public what the appropriate test would be in the case above, where real damage, for example, is done to the band.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, the PHCs and the speed at which they are expected to deal with falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A key feature of the Bill is the adoption of simplified procedures involving a straightforward claims form for victims of harassment and doing away with having to initiate an application through an originating summons, something which, more often than not, requires the hiring of a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is to be welcomed, especially for those who seek urgent relief.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second important feature of the Bill is the speed at which the PHCs will hear applications.
