speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have one clarification in this regard, and this is not with respect to EPOs, but to victims of falsehoods online where virality is a real concern and applicants can rely on a variety of remedies under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MinLaw has stated, and I quote, "Courts will be empowered to make relevant interim orders to provide victims with urgent relief".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was in the statement released on 1 April after the First Reading of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was not made clear how long that timeline would be.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I understand the Minister has now clarified that it would follow the regime under the EPOs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, let me use an example to suggest why, in certain cases, this may not be satisfactory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It follows, therefore, that a company in the Minister's example, the bitcoin company, provided that it was domiciled in Singapore, could apply urgently to the PHCs for perhaps a general correction order to arrest further damage which gives the Court powers to make the appropriate order or the applicant could rely on the other remedies available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The term here is the "expedited relief" that is sought.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a scenario, how quickly will the Courts hear such an application, given that significant damage, using the Minister's example, can occur within four to five hours?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or does the Bill envisage a faster hearing for the applicant, given that the death of a founder who has actually not died would easily meet the prima facie threshold of an interim order?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, it would appear that in some cases, the Courts may have to move faster on online falsehoods affecting individuals and companies and hear applications perhaps in even less than 24 hours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is such a shorter application hearing timeline within the contemplation of the Bill for individuals or entities who seek very urgent relief, failing which significant damage or losses would inevitably increase with every passing hour?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, how quickly can the public expect the PHCs to hear an interim application in the case of an online falsehood against an individual or entity?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And more generally and equally important, would the remedies provided for false statements in such a scenario necessitate filing a summons and affidavit, as is currently the case, or does the Ministry seek to introduce a quicker and simpler filing procedure akin to a simple form as envisaged for EPOs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are far-reaching remedies, largely identical to those the Government has sought under POFMA, and they can be imposed upon any individual or entity and applied for by the same.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While much of the attention of the public has been focused on POFMA since the First Readings of both Bills, but for the man on the street, POHA will be the law they can avail themselves to, with a view to taking action against other individuals or entities who peddle falsehoods against them, in addition to applications against Internet intermediaries like technology companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the explanatory statement to the Bill at page 71 appears to suggest that costs can be ordered, regardless of what type of remedy is ordered by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there any particular reason why the clause, as drafted, does not order costs against authors or publishers of false statements of fact in cases where the Courts issue orders other than correction orders, such as stop publication orders?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, can the Minister share in what circumstances and scenarios would the Court mandate costs against the subject who applied for the order as provided in clause 16CA(c)?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a matter of principle, why ought this to be the case?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods noted the observations of some representors that governments can also communicate falsehoods or misleading information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are enough examples of governments around the world through the course of history that have done so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why should the public not receive protection provided by this Bill against a prospective government or minister that uses his or her powers not just unwisely but maliciously, with a view to seek a remedy from a neutral body like the Courts, the same remedies which the Government can direct against individuals and companies under POFMA?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, it does not conform to the principle that the rule of law applies equally to all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate the point, in late 2014 and 2015, the New Mandala, a publication of the Australian National University, ran a series of exchanges between the former Singapore Ambassador to Australia Mr Burhan Gafoor and former Internal Security Act (ISA) detainee Dr Poh Soo Kai.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One aspect of the exchange involved the alleged assistance given by Dr Poh to an injured Communist Party of Malaysia bomber who escaped the premature detonation of an explosive device in a car along Still Road in 1974.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last week, Function 8, a local civil society organisation, put up a video titled "Fake News: Who is the culprit?" on its Facebook page.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In it, Dr Poh accused the Government of wrongfully alleging that he rendered assistance to the injured bomber in Masai, Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Dr Poh's position was that he never went across to Malaysia to render assistance to the injured party, something the Government has accused him of doing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Dr Poh further asserts that this can be proven in his favour through immigration records.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By alleging that he did go to Malaysia, Dr Poh then goes on to accuse the Government of peddling a false statement of fact as defined by the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the public interest not be better served in allowing a person to apply for the appropriate order from the PHCs and, in doing so, make their case?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would argue that the prospects of such recourse and the availability of a neutral forum like the Courts, combined with a simple process, would, in itself, act as a deterrent against individuals who seek to retrospectively burnish their reputations or embarrass the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, in the event an individual can apply for a stop publication or correction order under the new section 15, but he or she does not, and instead continues to accuse the Government, then an obvious adverse inference can be drawn about what the truth really is.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because all the relevant information is not publicly accessible, there is no way members of the public can objectively take a view on either side of the story.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has made its position known on matters involving the opening of the archives and a Freedom of Information regime in Parliament before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But these are not matters within the boundaries of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to having my clarifications addressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I made a comment about Central Provident Fund (CPF) policy that was taken out of context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: People thought I wanted the Government to stop them from using their existing CPF money for housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A Facebook post to that effect went viral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure Members can now infer why people hated me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware that many Members have had similar experiences receiving abuse online, as have others in the public eye.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I hope Members were prepared for the immense stream of criticism – some reasonable, some not; some gentle, some violent – that flows your way online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It was an unpleasant experience that I do not wish to recall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I share it today because I think it illustrates an important principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the law exists to provide justice, justice also requires that we play our part in understanding the limits of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A victim is the only one who can decide whether the law is the best recourse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there are many reasons why people feel the need to spew invective online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The law is not always necessary to effect a good outcome for all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, a reporter from the Straits Times contacted me to ask for my views on the President’s Address to Parliament which was delivered on 7 May 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That address called for bold changes and strong steps to address the challenges facing Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As I have some expertise on social security, I spoke on the role that CPF plays in providing both retirement and housing security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I was concerned that some Singaporeans might be over-investing in housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the event, what made it through to The Straits Times was my comment on ending the use of CPF for housing, and not the full reasoning behind it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not blame the reporter in the least because article space is scarce and many other experts were interviewed for a short article.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If my comment had remained in the pages of The Straits Times, that would have been the end of it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, someone from a website called Sure Boh Singapore found my CPF policy suggestion interesting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The post asks if Singaporeans who are made homeless by my CPF policy suggestion should sleep in my house.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I am sure there were more shares of different versions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: At some point, people even got confused and thought that the President or the Government were responsible for these suggestions on ending the use of CPF for housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I provided some examples of the comments people left on the Sure Boh Singapore post.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: You will notice people do not think much of my haircut.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Plenty of insults on my appearance, on my qualifications, a few outright threats of violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Of course, there were also more considered arguments, which I did not show here, and some who tried to appreciate the broader context of my views on CPF and housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Were there any real risks to my personal safety?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: As a university academic, where I work is public knowledge, and we have a fairly open campus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The staff could not find me so they sent him away.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: It turned out he had come to complain about my dangerous views on CPF, to me in person, or perhaps to the university management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: It turned out he was not unreasonable, just misinformed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But it did cross my mind that perhaps not all unexpected visitors might be reasonable people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But more importantly, there was an opportunity to engage people in a discussion on what CPF policy should be and what are the tradeoffs involved in the home financing decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, I contacted the various parties to set the story straight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I want to put on record my thanks to all parties for helping me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I was not a Nominated Member of Parliament back then, so it is not a question of influence, it is just people doing the right thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Yes, I received some unreasonable insults and jokes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But I also had a large number of people willing to engage with me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I will not say I convinced all of them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: What is more important is that we had an honest dialogue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: If there had been specific threats against my family or friends, I think it would have been quite right to refer the matter to the Police.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Fortunately, I do not think anybody made such threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: And the random threats of simple assault, frankly, I did not take too seriously, and they were really not as hurtful as the ones who took the time and creativity to insult me further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: It was an important lesson in not taking myself too seriously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We must treat one another with dignity online and offline, no matter our political disagreements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: And if we fall short, I hope that we will be treated with grace by the parties that we are offending.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These numbers reflect that the Act had been well-utilised over the few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, happy to hear that there will be enhancements to the Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Going through the Court process can be very daunting for lay persons.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, imperative that processes are kept simple and timelines are expedited.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It would help if the PHC becomes a one-stop "shop" where victims of harassment can get support with the Court proceedings, and even help with counselling or enforcement procedures, to ensure a meaningful remedy under POHA.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope this is what is envisioned under this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The harsh reality is that any order made under POHA will be a paper order.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Whether it truly affords protection will depend on whether there is support by the whole ecosystem, the Police, the Court staff and social workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, important to provide holistic support to the victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask if any measures are in place to ensure that victims of harassment and abuse are given sufficient assistance when they approach the Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would also like to make reference to the judge-led approach at the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Basically, one judge oversees all matters relating to the same parties and it allows for the judge to have a holistic understanding of the parties’ case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The judge-led approach also allows the Courts greater control over proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would, therefore, like to know if there are plans for the PHCs to employ the judge-led approach.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, Mr Speaker, I would like to continue my speech in Malay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   The advent of technology has transformed the way we live.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Social media has become an important channel for us to communicate and interact with one another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So much interaction takes place in social media to the point that it has led to the creation of an ecosystem and a different world online, which has become the place where we study, chat, trade, find love and to do many other things, and now, certain norms have also come into existence in the cyber world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important for us to ensure that we continue to uphold societal values by having certain rules online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Any negative actions that are unacceptable to us in the real world should similarly be unacceptable on the Internet.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my view, certain rules and ethics can exist by educating all online users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, we know that, sometimes, legislation and monitoring are required to ensure that everyone displays a positive behaviour on the Internet.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One issue being raised in today's Bill is doxxing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This term refers to the action of searching and publishing someone's personal information, usually with malicious intent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a growing trend on the Internet.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This usually happens when an individual did something that the general public finds unacceptable and the person's actions become viral online, usually in the form of a video.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some people who receive such information may feel triggered by what happened and begin to look for information on the supposedly errant individual.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Information about the person's name, home address, place of study or work is then displayed to the public on the Internet with the intent to shame the person and invite others to collectively condemn that individual's actions and take revenge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There may be those who ask, what is wrong with doxxing?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps they feel that there is nothing wrong with upholding the truth and getting back at the person who did something wrong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think we need to be clear about the negative impact of doxxing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is our intention if we make someone's personal information public?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What do we hope will happen and what is the impact on the individual and his or her family?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Is this the kind of healthy behaviour we want to see on the Internet and in real life?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Just imagine, if we use a real-world example, the act of doxxing is akin to printing the individual's photos and personal information and then placing it all in everyone's mailbox.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is the same as using paint to display information about an individual on the walls of public areas and telling everyone about what he or she did.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): For the reasons set out in my Malay speech, I am supportive of the proposed amendments in relation to making doxxing an offence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that if a certain conduct is unacceptable offline, it should not be permissible online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would, however, like to seek clarification on the application of the new laws.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe many Internet users especially, may want to know if they are committing an offence, given the prevalence of such acts online now.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Would an individual who has published the details about the target person, but without making any further statement urging action to be taken against him or her, be able to argue in defence that there was no intention to cause harm, but just to share information?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am also curious as to how enforcement will take place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Harassment, online or offline, is not acceptable behaviour.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It impinges on the personal rights of an individual and can have severe repercussions on the victims’ physical as well as mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that this needs to be balanced with the need to ensure that the process is not abused and no unduly harsh penalties are imposed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that enactment of laws needs to be coupled with public education, and I hope we will continue with this effort to build a better community online and offline.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Online reputation management, online reputation repair, online image rehabilitation, these are jobs that indicate the importance that companies and individuals attach to their online reputations today.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The restoration of damaged online reputations has become a growing industry.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To date, doxxing has adversely affected many individuals worldwide and in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals who have been seen behaving in socially unacceptable or unlawful ways have been taken to task by online vigilantes.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These vigilantes mount campaigns to uncover personal information of individuals, such as phone numbers, addresses, workplaces and publish them online, thereby inviting possible harassment by the online masses.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Victims of doxxing have been known to receive verbal abuse and even death threats to themselves and their families.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, there are many reasons why the criminalisation of doxxing is both crucial and timely.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In the first instance, doxxing, even when undertaken by seemingly well-intentioned online vigilantes, is often fraught with error.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Online vigilantes have been praised for their heroism and for helping to bring criminals to justice.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But their actions can also lead to the misidentification of individuals, with harmful consequences, especially when these vigilantes rush to "mete out justice".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Using only partial information shared via social media, including grainy videos and blurry photographs, the chances of erroneous identification are high.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The wrongly identified woman recounted her ordeal in her Facebook post, calling it "an emotional period and scary moment".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such mistaken identification can lead to incalculable emotional and financial costs for the unfortunate victims.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Even when the right individuals are correctly identified, it is unfair to have them harassed in this manner when they have yet to offer their side of the story.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But they are sentenced prematurely by the court of public opinion in a manner that can be disproportionately harsh.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the equivalent Chinese term for doxxing is "renrou sousuo" 人肉搜索 or "human flesh search engine".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This term graphically captures the rabid zeal with which online vigilantes hunt down and tear apart their targets.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Mobile phone shop owner Jover Chew may have been despicable in making his customer kneel and plead for a refund.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: However, when netizens published all the personal details of him and his wife, forcing them to go into hiding, their boorish behaviour was just as questionable.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In a society that is so connected, we cannot create a climate where online vigilantism is allowed to run riot and let the ferocity of the online mob inflict damage on individuals.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We should not permit mob mentality to take root and be the first recourse for justice.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Members of the public must also be educated that if they have evidence on any crimes or misdeeds, that they should turn it over to the Police rather than take matters into their own hands through doxxing.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we are transitioning towards a world which is increasingly powered by algorithms.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Processes, such as college admissions, job applications and even insurance premium pricing, will progressively include more aspects of automated decision making.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Automated searches of individuals' online profiles will play a bigger role in helping companies and organisations assess people.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Research has found that many existing algorithmically-driven decision-making systems offer little room for recourse in situations of error.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals seeking redress must invest considerable resources, with little guarantee of success.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Given such emerging circumstances, if someone’s online reputation is irretrievably damaged by doxxing, it will significantly hamper his or her existence in far-reaching ways and with life-long consequences.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In as much as I support the inclusion of doxxing as a crime in the amendment to POHA, I would also like to raise my concerns about the new remedies for victims of falsehoods.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Obviously, in light of the earlier points I made about the importance of our online reputations, I welcome the introduction of new remedies for victims of falsehoods.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to seek clarifications from the Minister about targeted and general correction orders.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to hearing the Minister's clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fake news is not only a political problem; it can also hurt businesses in Singapore, especially smaller ones, which have no resources to take swift remedial action to stop the damage.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whether these are attacks from their competitors, angry customers or pranksters, fake news can cause adverse impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Small businesses are more affected as they do not have the resources to react to fake news about their businesses.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In that episode, Bata was forced to withdraw 70,000 pairs of its B-First school shoes from its stores in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Not only was money lost, the image of the company suffered as well.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong mentioned, even local supermarket chain National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) FairPrice became a victim of fake news about its housebrand Jasmine fragrant rice being made of plastic.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, I am glad that businesses can now rely on the Act to protect themselves from fake news.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Or is it a case where the victim would still have to hire his own lawyer to apply for a stop publication order or correction order?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Minister can clarify how having the PHC to hear both criminal and civil matters can make it easier and less costly for the victim of fake news to control the damage caused as well as seek damages and redress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It reflects a deeper commitment to the protection and support for the vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are also debating this Bill at a time when a case of sexual voyeurism on university grounds has raised important and pressing questions about legal protection and institutional support for survivors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must use the current focus on harassment to have a meaningful national conversation on how we can create a society that does not tolerate any form of harassment, one where bystanders feel equipped to intervene and survivors feel empowered to seek justice.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, these amendments will not fulfil their mission.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I commend this amendment to make the process expeditious as well as more economical and accessible, which helps to make the ordeal less alienating and intimidating for the applicant.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lina is a survivor who did not submit her case to Court because the process is currently complicated and costly.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In her words, I quote, "I’m still struggling to rebuild my life….   so much paperwork, and I   need to take leave to go down to the Court so many times… It was too much for me." These changes will help individuals like Lina seek justice against their perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I think a $200 fee has also been cited.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Young adults under the age of 21 cannot seek POs under POHA unless a guardian makes the application on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This can be a deterrent from seeking legal redress for intimate partner violence and sexual harassment, even if social service agencies or law firms are involved.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Tina, not her real name, was 20 when she approached the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) about a blackmail case.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The perpetrator was threatening to leak explicit photos and videos of her if she did not continue to send him more.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the mental and emotional distress she was going through, she insisted on not involving her parents because she believed they would react "badly".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, she preferred waiting a whole year to turn 21 so that she could go to the Court alone.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Tina’s concerns are echoed by many, and they reflect a gap in the current system.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Tina’s story is not the only one I know.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The 18-year-old student I was mentoring a few years back was sexually harassed by her best friend’s brother and did not seek protection either because she did not want to let her parents know or they still do not till today.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that barriers for 16- to 21-year-olds can be removed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If need be, we could appoint social workers or Court counsellors to support applications in place of the survivor’s parents or guardian.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be cognisant of the social pressures that survivors might face and understand that some may not be ready to involve their family.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill defines these vulnerable persons as those with mental, physical disabilities and victims in an intimate relationship with the perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These changes recognise that these persons are especially vulnerable to being targeted for harassment, potentially face greater psychological and physical damage from such harassment, and are less able to defend themselves or prevent such harassment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard many bullying and harassment stories from just amongst my deaf friends and persons with mental health conditions whom I work with.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These extra consideration and attention are definitely a progressive yet necessary step forward.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But I cannot emphasise enough that the protection of the differently-abled must not only come from the law.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The continued harassment of these individuals originates from a deeper prejudice within our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue our whole-of-society efforts to tackle the root of this stigma and establish a widespread agreement to care and support the differently-abled.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are valid concerns to be raised on the effectiveness of enhanced punishments in administering two key areas of justice, namely, deterrence and retribution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Extensive studies reflect that enhanced punishments do not necessarily create a greater deterrent effect and may, in fact, be counter-productive.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Research done by the Centre for Criminal Justice Studies in Canada has shown that longer sentences and harsher punishments do not reduce the rates of sexual crimes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, the reverse may be observed, where longer sentences increased recidivism due to a lack of repentance for the initial crime, as reported by the National Research Council in the United States.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, enhanced punishments may even counter-productively discourage the victim from reporting instances of harassment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In eight out of 10 cases that AWARE’s Sexual Assault Care Centre sees, survivors know or are close to their perpetrators.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, especially when the perpetrator is a family member, enhanced punishments may heighten the fears of destroying the perpetrator’s life, deterring survivors from reporting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Jenny, for example, shared that even if the perpetrator, her father, was jailed for the maximum period of time, he would never feel the fear, shame, terror and disgust that she has had to deal with throughout her childhood and into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She also shared that her mother would not be able bear the guilt and it would devastate her, I quote, "so punishing him even for the longest time would only bring more pain", unquote.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In 2017, the United Nations Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women Committee (CEDAW) made a similar recommendation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also urge the Government to consider and look into the deterrent effects of other measures like community service and restorative justice measures as restitutionary agreements.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to clarify if the protection that is now available to entities also creates an equal responsibility for them to exercise reasonable care to prevent and correct promptly any harassing behaviour, failing which, they would be held liable for their employees’ actions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The sexual voyeurism case I mentioned at the start of my speech raises questions about organisational investigation processes, support offered to complainants, and helpful prevention programmes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Although not legally enforceable, the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment provides important guidelines on these issues but it is unclear if the Advisory covers institutes of higher learning (IHLs).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The changes made in this Bill are driven by key principles that should be celebrated, especially in the clear commitment towards protecting and supporting the most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, Mr Speaker, we must remember that legislative changes cannot be the end of the process of change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the Ministry spares no effort in education and awareness efforts with schools, IHLs, workplaces and communities so that every member of our society knows not just what their rights are but also how to activate these rights in the face of bullying and harassment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Social support must be enhanced to ensure victims have an accessible and holistic process of recovery from these traumas.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And more importantly, we must continue to spare no effort at every level to build a society with values of respect and inclusivity that will discourage these crimes against the vulnerable in the first place.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because a society that has more justice and compassion needs less charity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And our great hope in such a society is in individual character.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, Mr Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Every now and then, there will be online news about people who have done something seemingly wrong, followed by doxxing on these people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Their personal information will be put online, including their home address, work address or their telephone numbers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Quite often, the one being searched out turns out to be the wrong person.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even if it is, indeed, that person, we should not harass him.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we can hurt someone just because we do not like his behaviour, then we are no different from a primitive society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is more, the people living with them, including the elderly and their children, are equally harassed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is one of the first countries in the world to illegalise doxxing and I am very proud of this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also want to remind everyone not to go online and publicise your personal information.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is also known as doxxing and often leads to harassment and harm of individuals in real life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Doxxing is certainly not a foreign concept to Singapore’s cybersphere.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are communities and forums dedicated to "CSI", a term they use which refers to investigating the victim and publishing his or her personal information online.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am proud that Singapore is the first country to make the act of doxxing a criminal offence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have had our own social vigilantism gone wrong incidents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even if the people are correctly identified, harassing and harming them is never justified.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If someone has done something objectionable, we can deal with it through our laws.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we cannot allow people to harass them in real life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That is like taking justice into our own hands, no different from secret societies or prehistoric villagers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Regardless of whether the target of doxxing was innocent or guilty of the allegation against him, the consequences of doxxing can be disproportionate and may plague the victims for life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is the saying, "The Internet never forgets." When information goes viral on the Internet, even if you remove the source material, the other people who have seen it would have remembered it and even made copies to share it around.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even when clarifications are made, these may never reach the people who have seen the original mistaken source.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Jon Ronson’s book "So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed" documents the stories of doxxing victims who continue to live in fear of harassment and prejudice even years after the doxxing happened.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of them had their employment prospects hurt.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most of them had not actually hurt anyone or committed crimes to deserve all these.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And those innocent people who live with them, including elderly and children, are put through hell, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Not everyone who gets doxxed is even suspected of doing something wrong.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are whole accounts dedicated to taking pictures of women without consent and talking about them in a sexual way.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For some women, people have found their social media accounts and, from there, their personal information, and harassed them in real life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I hope more can be done to educate individuals to be careful with their personal information and photos.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This includes having the correct privacy settings for information like home addresses and phone numbers on social media accounts, erasing location information on photos when sharing them on social media, and not sharing compromising photographs and information publicly or with people they do not know well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Social vigilantism has been referred to as a perilous form of justice.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I wonder if it can even be considered a form of justice when it simply creates chaos and fear in many cases.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge all those who truly value justice to consider joining the Police Force, where you can put your "CSI" skills to good use.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is no need to take matters into your own hands and risk causing irreversible damage to innocent lives in the process.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, I would like to highlight another type of harassment, that is, harassment by ex-employer using WhatsApp and emails.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I received an email from my resident asking for help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Subsequently, I met up with her at my Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She looked like in her late 20s, and she told me that she gets her new job through her friend and this company is dealing with blockchain technology and cryptocurrency.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, her job is to sell cryptocurrency to as many customers as possible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She has to do a lot of networking, has to see many customers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the first day of her work, her boss added her into many WhatsApp groups.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She wanted to quit but she was persuaded to stay on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Then, two weeks into the job, she decided to quit because she found out about her boss' "hire and fire", and there were a lot of people being fired before she was hired.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, she sent an email to her boss to inform her boss that she wanted to quit with immediate effect.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Soon after that, she started receiving WhatsApp messages and emails from her ex-boss.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, you have to pay the company one month's salary." She has been working there for two weeks and she was not paid.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just a few days ago, on 2 May, she received one more email.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is very painful to see young ladies being harassed, being tortured like this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It so happens that they are young, beautiful ladies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of these cases are just plain bullying, others involve manipulation with criminal intent, and yet others are carried out in the name of justice or "vigilantism".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we understand that people generally want justice to be done, they must understand that it would be best to leave it to the relevant authorities to perform thorough investigations and follow-ups.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, many Internet users may be too quick to present information without having the full facts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government should educate members of the public about appropriate actions they can take and how to share information with the relevant agencies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to build trust and increase the public’s confidence, the informed agencies should also share investigation results and outcomes, where circumstances allow, with concerned members of the public, so that they would not feel that all their cooperative efforts have gone down a deep black hole.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As time goes on, the public will trust in the Government to take the right and calibrated actions and be less inclined to administer their own brands of justice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such acts are tantamount to the "warrant to kill" order practised by the triads and secret society in the old days, which should not be allowed to have place in our society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, we should consider the harm caused to innocent parties, especially those who have been framed and set up.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This reminds me of a friend who was humiliated and threatened with breaches of privacy by her ex-husband after their marriage turned sour.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, this Bill is very timely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure that many of our Members here have similar experiences where residents come to them for help about cyberbullying.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot allow cyberbulling to threaten public and individual safety.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although they claim that they do this for justice, they must respect our law and to pass the matter over to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no need to get the innocent involved.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): With that, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is critical that the avenues to seek relief and redress are not fraught with complexity or lead to a sense of futility or, worse, where the victim of harassment perceives himself or herself to be further victimised.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I will be addressing these points in relation to: one, anonymous harassers; two, intimate harassers; three, workplace harassers; and four, the management of harassment cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One of the challenges to the ability of the victim to take any action against a perpetrator is the lack of knowledge of the perpetrator’s identity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Take, for example, a female victim who was harassed online by persons unknown to her.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These persons had posted hateful messages directed at her, revealed her contact number online while threatening that they were closing in on her residence and posted her contact details on online sex forums offering sexual services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Worried for her safety and her family’s safety, the victim reported the matter to the Police but was told that there was nothing further that the Police could do as they needed real names and contact numbers before they could proceed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This same example may happen to a male victim as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the Bill now provides for the application of stop publication orders to prohibit the publication of false statement of facts, these unknown perpetrators can easily put up other false information of the victim on other platforms to continue harassing the victim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some of these persons also deliberately mask their identities and Internet Protocol addresses to avoid detection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The anonymity of the harassers adds to the sense of loss of control and fear already experienced by victims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The anonymous harassers may pose threats of violence or incite violence by others on the victims and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The victims have no means of assessing if the harasser or persons will carry out the threats of violence, or who they should be guarding against.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This creates a significant amount of stress on the victims, which can be debilitating.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this regard, the law enforcement agencies must strengthen their capabilities in identifying these unknown perpetrators to send a strong message to these harassers that they cannot get away with such behaviour.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Intimate harassers can inflict even more pain and anguish on their victims and even persons related to the victims, due to the increased vulnerability and proximity of the victim in the intimate relationship.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The intimate harasser has access to private and intimate information of the victim which can enable the intimate harasser to hold the victim to ransom and force the victim to acquiesce to the harasser’s demands.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workplace harassment involving cases of rage and aggression by members of the public against persons in public-facing frontline jobs is on the rise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Last month, a man was caught on camera punching a 60-year-old private security supervisor at Roxy Square allegedly over seeking of directions out of the building.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The security supervisor fell and suffered a swollen eye and a sprained neck.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While these private security officers work in private spaces, their work, in effect, straddles the line delineating private and public spaces as provided in the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Given the recent introduction of criminal penalties regulating the conduct of private security officers to boost the industry's professionalism and bolster Singapore's defences, it is timely to review the according of special protection to this group of workers under POHA beyond what is currently provided for under the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I raised this on several occasions in this House on behalf of these workers who undertake public-facing jobs and who may be exposed to harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They include private security officers, cleaners, transport workers as well as healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Harassment cannot be condoned nor accepted as part and parcel of these public-facing jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Through the Legal Clinics and Legal Primers organised by NTUC, union members are provided with access to support, resources and the expertise of legal professionals, social workers and counsellors to prevent and manage workplace harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At these sessions, workers have shared personal encounters of harassment at the workplace, ranging from physical to verbal harassment, some of a sexual nature.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A dipstick poll at one such Legal Primer indicated that 20% of respondents had encountered workplace harassment of a sexual nature before.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Name calling and hurling vulgarities were also commonplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In some cases, harassers used physical force to intimidate victims by blocking their way or even by pushing and shoving.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: She was advised to seek recourse under POHA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Victims of workplace harassment often find it difficult to speak up because they may be fearful of losing their jobs, receiving a bad appraisal, perceived as not going along with the office culture or blaming themselves.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workplace harassment can impact the victim psychologically and physically and his or her ability to work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad that MinLaw has, at the Committee of Supply Debate 2019, taken note of my suggestion to track the types of POHA cases filed and that the Ministry will be working with the State Courts to explore this further.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Information gleaned from workplace harassment POHA cases can help in the refinement of the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment to better prevent and manage harassment at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Falsehoods can damage their business reputation and have knock-on effects on the workers' livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The relevant authorities had investigated the claims and found the allegations to be untrue.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Not only do these falsehoods cause unnecessary alarm and confusion among the public, the reputation of the business and their workers' livelihoods would also be impacted, in the event where the public chooses to boycott the business due to the falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In cases of prolonged and sustained harassment, victims can feel compelled to make drastic changes to their way of life, including moving houses, changing jobs and cutting themselves off from social media and social engagements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Victims undergo significant stress, experience a sense of loss and powerlessness and a pervasive sense of insecurity, even in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It takes courage for victims to take action against their harassers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is at the risk of further incurring the wrath of the harasser and being subject to even greater harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Care must be taken to minimise inadvertent victim-blaming in the course of investigative and legal inquiry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The victim should also be kept informed of developments in investigations at appropriate junctures.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To help victims to get back on their feet and prepare for any backlash from harassers, the Police and the newly set up PHC should direct victims to specialised counsellors or social workers to assist victims in drawing up safety plans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In putting together a personalised safety plan, victims can identify concrete steps they can take to better protect themselves, along with resources they can tap on to seek help.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These safety plans can help victims to gain a sense of control over the situation and better cope with the investigative and legal processes to follow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With these submissions and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the aims of the amendment Bill which was carefully outlined by the hon Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong in his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I commend MinLaw for taking active steps to protect victims of harassment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe, once passed, this Bill will have the effect of considerably strengthening the protection regime for victims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have four comments to make on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many hon Members spoke about this before me.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think there is clearly support for the criminalisation of such behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The query, though, is on the ambit of the proposed crime and, in that, I join the observations made by the hon Member Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He mentioned an example where an author posts information online to highlight a person's offending conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The author's focus is not necessarily to harass the person but to highlight the person's bad conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It, however, may be foreseeable that the person may still be harassed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Alternatively, there could be situations where a victim of an offence shares his or her experience online and names the perpetrator at the same time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such situations, would the offence of doxxing be committed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that case, the defendant was a psychotic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He targeted the plaintiff company's employees, particularly the women, and repeatedly sent emails and made calls to them using vulgar and threatening language.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The company obtained an interim injunction preventing the defendant from harassing its employees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, it failed to get a permanent injunction as the High Court doubted the existence of the common law tort of harassment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The common law tort of harassment has since been abrogated by POHA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It would be good for employers to be provided with such remedies for two main reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, as an employer, the company has a duty to its employees to provide a safe working environment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member, Mr Patrick Tay, was talking about workplace harassment just a few minutes ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, it has a direct interest in ensuring that its employees are not harassed at work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, when we are dealing with a company with many employees, the harasser can escape the effect of an injunction by shifting the target to employees whom he has not harassed before.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the provision is widened to allow the company to commence civil action against the harasser and obtain an injunction to prevent harassment, it can protect all its employees in one go.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the 2005 English High Court decision of First Global Locums, the High Court granted an injunction under the UK Protection from Harassment Act in favour of a recruitment company against a disgruntled ex-employee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In deciding to issue an injunction protecting the company, the Court held that if it only covered the employees who had been harassed without including the company, there is a likelihood for the ex-employee to harass other employees of the company who, at that point in time, have not been harassed yet and thereby retaliate against the company.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the hon Senior Minister of State's clarification on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My next point deals with the ambit of the protection order under the proposed section 12 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As currently worded, the scope of protection under the order would involve prohibiting the harasser from doing anything in relation to the victim and this right may extend to directing that the harasser be excluded from occupying the shared residence with the victim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It also may include requiring the harasser to stop publishing an offending communication or referring the harasser to attend counselling and mediation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State also mentioned some other aspects of broadening the PO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From time to time, we read of cases of female victims being harassed by ex-boyfriends who possess videos of them being intimate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On such occasions, victims may, and indeed have, taken action under POHA to obtain a PO against the respondents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is important because so long as the videos are in the hands of the harasser, there is every chance that offending behaviour may reoccur.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would have imagined that the Court should have such powers to ensure that the objective of the PO is met.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the hon Senior Minister of State's clarification on this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From my reading of the proposed section 17 of POHA, it seems that there may not be jurisdiction to deal with a situation where the victim of harassment is outside Singapore at the material time and the act of harassment by the harasser is committed outside Singapore, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate why there should not be criminal jurisdiction over such acts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, when it comes to civil jurisdiction, I would respectfully suggest different considerations should apply.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding my comments, I wholeheartedly support the amendment Bill.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the key amendments of this Bill is the establishment of the specialist Court, the PHC, which will provide a one-stop centre for all matters relating to protection from harassment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This arrangement will certainly facilitate the provision of holistic and effective interventions for victims.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The decision to permit the PHC not to be bounded by the rules of evidence in the conduct of civil proceedings will also be very helpful for victims.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would like, however, to seek some clarifications on the enforcement of POs once issued.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill indicates that remedies and recourse for breaches of POs and EPOs will be strengthened.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is that these are implemented after the breaches, by which time the victims would have suffered another round of psychological or physical trauma.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In cases where the accused may be unable to think rationally nor behave with restraint, there seems little to prevent them from causing more trouble.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have encountered some of these cases in my dealings as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, we had a daughter and her mother who felt they were threatened by one of their sons.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although I do not have the full information about the case, it was clear that they felt that this son was not behaving rationally and they were in constant fear of being attacked or harassed by this son, despite the existence of POs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And there was very little, in terms of immediate recourse, that they could turn to.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, is it possible to introduce stronger deterrent measures to enforce the POs and can more be done to prevent subsequent harassments or attacks?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, like many Members before me, I do welcome the amendments to counter the unfortunate new social trend of doxxing, where people’s personal information, such as names, photographs, contact details, home and work addresses, are shared online in order to facilitate harassment, issue threats or cause physical harm.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many examples have been shared in this House over the past hour.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I myself have also encountered such examples, maybe not of such degree or this nature.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, several months ago, I came across a cleaner in one of the hawker centres who had a little bit of disagreement with one of his customers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It so transpired that the details about the cleaner were then posted on social media which led to a lot of consternation to this cleaner.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, notwithstanding the merits or the lack thereof of the case, I think these are very unfortunate developments in the social media arena.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these acts of online "vigilantism", such as to expose the couple who harassed an old man at a hawker centre, inconsiderate and dangerous drivers, voyeurs and Peeping Toms, may seem warranted but, in fact, undermines the very foundation of our justice system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Administering justice is not an activity which can be done part-time, remotely nor casually.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thorough investigations of the facts of the events are necessary, in fairness to all parties involved.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A number of netizens resort to doxxing because they lack confidence in Government institutions to rectify certain situations and social behaviours, leading them to take matters into their own hands.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important that public institutions concerned show their awareness of these incidents and prove that the Government takes a serious view of their feedback through comprehensive measures and consistent enforcement.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Public education to increase their awareness of the appropriate forums to share such information is essential.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, they should be encouraged to post and share videos of, for example, dangerous driving with the Traffic Police, forward information on disputes to the relevant authorities and share information with emergency services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In order to reduce the incidents of doxxing, public institutions must be prepared to step up to address public concerns expeditiously and provide updates on actions taken.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That being said, I would like to make some recommendations to better support victims by improving responses of enforcement personnel and by increasing the use of counselling and mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to seek clarifications on the scope of the new offence of doxxing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the online talk show series "Under the Carpet", Debra Tang highlighted the need to train first responders on the handling of harassment, assault and violence cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From her interviews on the show, she noted that, "Too often, victims are made to feel ashamed, foolish or disbelieved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many go away wishing they had never made a complaint or reached out for help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And, if it should happen again, they will never speak up." It also emerged through the show that there have been instances where victims felt that they were not taken seriously because they may not have exhibited behaviours that law enforcement deem "typical" of assault victims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The legislative amendments to strengthen protections under POHA will not amount to much without an environment where victims feel safe to speak up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Training our law enforcement officers to better manage these cases with tact and empathy is crucial in creating such an environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am aware that changes have been made by the Singapore Police Force to investigative processes and Court procedures in order to create a safer space for victims of sexual crimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm if such changes apply also to victims of harassment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Do Victim Care Officers, who are specially trained in victim care management, also handle victims of harassment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Physically restraining the harasser addresses the immediate threat posed by their harassing behaviour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, because the harasser will not be detained indefinitely, the victim remains at risk of their harassing behaviour after the harasser is released.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of my residents had a PPO against her husband.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They were going through a divorce and their relationship was tensed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In August, she was repeatedly stabbed by her husband in front of her youngest daughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her husband was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment but any punishment meted out can never heal the loss of a mother for their two daughters or undo the trauma suffered by the youngest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The PPO was insufficient to prevent her husband’s attack.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A social worker could consistently monitor and assess the case, and identify any worrying irregularities in a harasser's behaviour in advance to prevent ill-fated cases like that of my resident.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, when ordering POs or EPOs, the Court can include the condition that the respondent and victim attend counselling or mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the Bill introduces a new offence of doxxing which signals the Government's firm commitment towards addressing new and upcoming forms of harassment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially welcomed at a time where online vigilantism is becoming more rampant in our society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as mentioned by many in this House, there is some ambiguity as to what constitutes doxxing as defined under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many have shared examples and I will share, of course, one about an animal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2016, a story emerged on Facebook of a driver who ran over a dog from a dog shelter and drove off in a hit-and-run.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her vehicle plate number was posted on Facebook with a request for anyone who knew the identity of the driver to text or message a private number.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Netizens used the posted plate number to obtain and publish online the woman’s personal particulars.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The car owner and her employer were harassed online by angry netizens.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It subsequently emerged that the owner had, in fact, not been driving the vehicle at the time and did not run over the dog.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This story highlights the dangers of Internet vigilantism and the ambiguities in the definition of doxxing as an offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the initial action of publishing the woman's vehicle plate number on their Facebook page be considered doxxing?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, would a vehicle plate number fall under the definition of "identity information"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments include Illustration (d), which references a situation in which an individual X records a video of Y driving recklessly in a car and posts the video on an online forum.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While Illustration (d) goes on to state that no offence is committed because X posted the video with the intent to warn people to drive defensively, it is not clear from the example whether a vehicle plate number alone would constitute "identity information".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, was there intent to cause harm, alarm or distress in the situation where initially they were simply trying to find out who was driving the car and hit the dog?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the defence that the conduct was reasonable be raised here?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there was a request for help to identify the driver, it was also expressly stated that the information should be sent to a private number.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This story highlights my broader concern about the difficulty in determining whether there was intention to cause harm, alarm or distress by the publication of identity information, or whether the conduct was reasonable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parliament expressed a preference to leave interpretation of POHA to the Courts, as POHA offences are highly dependent on the factual matrix.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Courts have stated that intention, being a thought process, can only usually be proved by drawing inferences from the surrounding circumstances and the actions of the accused.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister shed more light on what the Courts should consider in drawing these inferences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can more examples of permissible and impermissible publication of identity information be provided either in the Minister’s response or through guidelines or informational material from the Ministry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will be helpful for guiding the conduct of the public who should not have to be hauled to Court before finding out whether their actions constitute an offence or not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it might be prudent to prohibit publication of these categories of information, regardless of intention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am grateful for the strong support that has been expressed in this House.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members have shared many examples of how Singaporeans – and animals – some known personally to them, have experienced harassment, both in the physical and the online space.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will do my best to respond but I cannot reply to all the examples that have been cited, some more graphically.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
