text: But the stories that Members have shared in this House illustrate just how easy it is to spread falsehoods about individuals, about businesses, and how there are serious consequences, immediate and downstream, and why we need this Bill to give redress and recourse for individuals against physical and online harassment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira shared a very vivid, and might I say graphic, example of his personal experience of being harassed and spoke passionately about the need for each of us to treat one another with dignity offline as well as online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I cannot agree more with Assoc Prof Walter Theseira.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members have vividly described falsehoods which have serious and devastating consequences, and which can also have a deep and long-lasting impact.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The questions that Members have raised can be categorised into various baskets and I intend to address them as comprehensively as I can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, let me address the Court process which various Members have touched on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court will consider each of these applications judiciously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These third parties, on top of being able to bring their application, can also give practical support to the victim by providing information on Court procedures and processes and also help, especially at an important time like this, on lending emotional and moral support to the victim during the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked whether there are measures in place to ensure victims of harassment and abuse are given sufficient assistance when they approach the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, in particular, expressed hope that the PHC will be a "one-stop shop" to provide practical support and help with counselling.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The current laws, augmented by the proposed revisions in this Bill, strive to make the process as easy as possible and as simple as possible for victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is also an assessor stationed there to look at the application, understand the nature of the application, and guide the applicant on the application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On top of that, options are also put to the applicant in the appropriate cases to consider counselling or mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, the Court already has the power to refer parties to counselling and mediation and will continue to do so in the appropriate cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The streamlining of procedures and expedited timelines that I mentioned in my earlier speech build on this to enhance the process even more.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In relation to the Police's investigations, Mr Louis Ng asked if Victim Care Officers who are specially trained in victim care management also handle the cases involving victims of harassment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Victim Care Cadre Programme is available to all victims of crime who require emotional support throughout the course of investigations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes victims of harassment who can avail themselves of victim care services by providing their consent to such services to investigation officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if it is possible to make it mandatory for the Court to consider referring parties to mediation and counselling.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But just to underscore the point, under section 12(2B), in appropriate cases, the Courts already do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have the power, and they do frequently arrange for parties to attend counselling or mediation, when it is appropriate in those cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if it is possible for social workers to be attached to applicants of POs in certain cases, so that the social worker can consistently monitor and be aware of the development of the case, and also be able to identify worrying trends or changes in the harasser's behaviour.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The case which Mr Louis Ng cited is a tragic one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I would say that there are already existing avenues of assistance for applicants for POs to onsite counsellors and also psychiatrists who will be able to assist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Separately, the amendments will also ensure that the respondent can be ordered to undergo a mental health assessment and the appropriate treatments where necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But nonetheless, Mr Louis Ng's suggestion is an interesting one and we will work with the relevant agencies to see how we can further consider this suggestion and also enhance the support to victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked if there are plans for the PHC to employ a judge-led approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And clause 24 of the Bill empowers the PHC precisely to adopt a judge-led approach in any civil proceedings before the Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will ensure that the judges can exercise greater control over proceedings, taking charge of the proceedings and managing it from the judge's perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The overarching objective of this is to ensure that the proceedings are dealt with as efficiently as possible, fairly, but also to ensure that acrimony is kept at as low a level as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza has asked about the timelines and asked how long the process to apply for a PO and EPO currently takes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He also asked what resources will be deployed to PHC to ensure that the proposed expedited timelines that we have in mind can be met.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it will be several weeks or, if not, months, downstream from the original application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will work with the State Courts to ensure that necessary resources are deployed to expedite the hearings of these applications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the intention of the PHC in the first place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Having a dedicated Court to hear these applications with streamlined procedures, applying them in a way that best suits the case, will make for expedition and also efficiency in managing the cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about a case where, on occasions, you might need to hear a case in five to six hours because of very pressing demands.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: No doubt, Courts will try, but I would say that it will be very difficult to do so mainly because to hear a case properly and fully, one will have to ensure that the proper evidence and the right materials are before the Courts for the Courts to make the proper assessment of the case and decide.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about jurisdiction, and I would just like to deal with that, the civil jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai suggested that our Courts should have the jurisdiction to hear civil applications where the victim of harassment is outside Singapore at the material time and where the act of harassment by the harasser is committed outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The basis of the Court's jurisdiction is as set out in section 17 of the existing POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That does not change, and we acknowledge that this limits the scope of jurisdiction in respect of acts which may take place overseas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There were questions relating to the measures that are available to enhance protection for victims of harassment, in particular, victims who are intimately related to the harasser.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All victims, whether married or not married, of whatever gender, will be protected under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to Mr Pritam Singh's point, the remedies are gender-neutral.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked if it is possible to introduce stronger deterrent measures to enforce POs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has also asked if more can be done to prevent subsequent harassments or attacks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill has several measures designed to deal with this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Two of them are deterrent in nature, and a third seeks to try to address the underlying cause or reason for the harassment conduct in the first place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mentioned that in my earlier speech, especially in a case where hurt is involved or where the harassing conduct persists even after the PO has been issued.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In these two cases, the breach of the PO is made arrestable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Previously, they were not and that might have accounted for why some victims felt reluctant to step forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second deterrent measure is to have enhanced penalties for offences which involved a second or subsequent breach of the POs and EPOs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 11, in this regard of the Bill, doubles the maximum penalty prescribed if a POHA offence is committed against an intimate partner or against a vulnerable person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The third measure seeks to address the underlying root cause of harassment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Dr Chia pointed out, there may be cases where the accused could not be acting rationally or thinking straight, or behaving with restraint.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We fully agree with this, as it also mirrors the feedback given to us by the various stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, separate criminal proceedings have to be brought so that a Mandatory Treatment Order can be granted upon a criminal conviction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are now empowering the Court to consider, upfront, where appropriate, whether the respondent should undergo psychiatric assessment and treatment after it grants a PO in civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, at the juncture that the Court considers that it is appropriate to grant the Order, it also has to look at whether or not psychiatric assessments and treatments might be necessary for this accused person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my view, this benefits the accused person, as early psychiatric intervention may help to prevent further harassment where the harassment is due to this underlying psychiatric condition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Anthea Ong observed that harsher punishments are not necessarily always an effective deterrent and may not serve victims better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We agree that increased punishments alone cannot be the only solution, and indeed, they are not the only solution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, as I mentioned earlier, apart from the Mandatory Treatment Orders and psychiatric assessments, it provides already for options for mediation and counselling.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And these are designed to ensure that, as far as possible, the process, where possible, keeps acrimony and the aggravation to a minimum.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for examples of situations where the enhanced penalties might not apply to a harasser in an intimate relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 11 sets out a non-exhaustive list of factors that the Court may have regard to when determining whether an accused person and the victim were in an intimate relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The list mirrors that introduced by the Criminal Law Reform Bill yesterday in respect of certain Penal Code offences committed in the context of intimate relationships.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill seeks to enhance protection for victims who are psychologically manipulated or intimidated by their intimate partners.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For some of these victims, stepping forward to seek help in the context of that relationship is very challenging.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And for other victims, sometimes, seeking help is not even an option at all.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the one hand, there is a need to protect such victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But equally, and on the other hand, we should ensure that not every offender is subject to enhanced penalties merely by reason of being in an intimate relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That provision is set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, on Mr Patrick Tay's example, if there is no evidence before the Court that there was an imbalance of power in the context of the relationship with one party being coercive, the other party being submissive, and no evidence that the victim was unable, by reason of the relationship, to prevent the harm that was caused or will be caused, then if an accused person commits an offence under POHA in this kind of scenario, the enhanced penalties will not apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for some recent data on the effectiveness of POs, the number of cases of repeated breaches and subsequent injuries or deaths.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These statistics give a snapshot, but, in themselves, cannot be considered to be an accurate barometer of the effectiveness of POs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai has raised a query which also pertains to the effectiveness of POs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has shared an example of a female victim who obtains a PO against her ex-boyfriend who has harassed her using intimate recordings that he possesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has sought clarification about whether section 12 prohibits the Court from making ancillary orders that it deems fit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The short answer is that section 12(3) provides that a PO may include any requirement necessary for or incidental to the proper carrying into effect of the order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it gives the Court some flexibility to consider all the facts and determine what is the appropriate remedy in the context of that case, given no two harassment cases will have similar facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested that the scope of "public service worker" under the Act be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, I think Mr Patrick Tay suggested that private security guards be accorded special protection under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We had considered this point before and I think Mr Patrick Tay is aware that this issue has come up in this House previously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To explain the current position, individuals are considered "public service workers" for the purpose of enhanced protection under POHA if their jobs serve the general public, and not just the patrons of a private business or establishment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We note the points that Mr Patrick Tay has made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Minister for Law had, in 2014, said that the precise classes of workers covered should evolve as the operating landscape of public service evolves over time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Offenders can also be prosecuted under the Penal Code for egregious cases involving hurt, criminal intimidation or criminal force.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the issue of harassment at the workplace, Ms Anthea Ong asked whether entities now have a responsibility to exercise reasonable care to prevent and correct the harassing behaviour of their employees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, employers already have a duty to ensure the safety and health of their employees at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments that we are proposing in the Bill today do not change that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment which was issued in 2015 stands as a practical guide and does so till today for employers and employees to better prevent and manage harassment at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add to this that the Bill provides that entities can be criminally liable for all the offences under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it applies to entities as well as to individuals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And for entities, because they are non-natural persons, the principles of attribution will apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if the officers managing a company instruct their employees to carry out acts of harassment, such as harassment in connection with moneylending activities, the company itself can be criminally liable for those acts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments will, therefore, discourage entities from using or allowing their employees or several employees to harass their customers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also raised an example of a disgruntled person who harassed the employees of a company by sending them repeated emails and also using threatening language.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think that is the case that went before the Courts some years ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has suggested that the company be allowed to commence an action to protect its employees from the harassing conduct of such a person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, as illustrated by Mr Murali Pillai’s example, the company and its employees are both victims for the purposes of section 3 of POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The company can apply for a PO under section 12.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the company is an entity, such a PO would also extend to its employees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the definition of the term "statement of fact" and if it is meant to be different from how the term is currently understood under section 15.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 3, which contains a definition of "statement of fact", is merely intended to make the definition of the term clearer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On this, Mr Pritam Singh also asked a question about the black metal band.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I forgot the precise language that the Member had used about the phraseology.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But from what I caught of the statement, it was an expression of an opinion as to the effects of attending black metal concerts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether you agree with that or not is a different issue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as I have mentioned at the start, a statement of fact does not include a statement of opinion or a commentary or even a critique.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Stating an opinion, without more, that black metal bands incite people to do violence – I think that was the thrust of the statement the Member mentioned – would not be a false statement of fact.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing has three queries relating to entities that are the subject of falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is because the remedies available under POHA seek to protect individuals and entities against false statements of fact by preventing or limiting the spread of those false statements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Remedies, such as correction orders and targeted correction orders, are also available to ensure that the false statements are corrected and made known to those who had viewed the false statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will allow the subject of the falsehood to seek the remedies provided under POHA as well as for damages under civil proceedings in one Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it makes the proceedings a lot more simplified and a lot more convenient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Mr Yee Chia Hsing has asked if a victim of a falsehood only needs to make a Police report and, I think in his words, "piggy-back" on criminal investigations in order to obtain an order in relation to the falsehood.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, the answer is no, and that is because the deeming provisions which allow a respondent to rely on a prior criminal conviction, apply only in relation to applications for POs or EPOs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They do not apply where a section 15 falsehood is concerned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in answer to Mr Yee's third question, that is the purpose of the amendments – to simplify, to expedite, to make it easier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think to Mr Pritam Singh's point, these simplified procedures also apply to falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For context, a Court must first be satisfied in such an application that there is prima facie evidence, amongst other things, that the publication of the specified material has caused or is likely to cause the subject of the false statement harm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An interim order under section 16 can be made only if it is just and equitable to do so in the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The harm need not be physical; it may be harm to the subject's reputation or business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And as we know, the nature of online falsehoods is that their effect often extends beyond the realm of physical harm, moving down to reputational or emotional harm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, indeed, the examples that we have heard in the House today by Members illustrate that where entities in particular are involved, the harm is often to their reputation or business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked about third party expenses in complying with and adhering to General Correction Orders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 20, which introduces the new section 16CA, allows for costs reasonably incurred by third parties in complying with a General Correction Order to be made against any of the following: the author of the false statement, provided that the author authorised or caused the statement to be published; any person or entity that intentionally published the false statement; and the applicant of the order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh also asked if this was intended to apply beyond the General Correction Order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason for clause 20 is that the General Correction Order brings in third parties – third party platforms which have got nothing to do with the publication, the authoring of the statement and are not the author itself; and it is in that situation that a cost remedy and regime are provided for in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not to say that this, otherwise, takes away the victim's ability under civil law to seek redress and that can include the costs of any suffering incurred by the victim against the publisher or by the author of the falsehood.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked about liability of third parties and let me just deal with that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is in the context of moderators of social media groups and platforms for posts made by users.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The position is that if the user made a post which falls foul of the law on doxxing, the moderator will not ipso facto be liable for doxxing since he himself has not published the information and Mr Pritam Singh's own example, as I understood his example having heard it, was that there was also no intention to harass in that case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to deal with Prof Lim Sun Sun's queries and there were two queries that came through.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is what the estimated volume of online falsehood cases that could be brought before the Courts after the Bill is passed; second, how significant an administrative cost this will be in the context of Internet intermediaries?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, I would say the point goes beyond just numbers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If, by these amendments, we allow more victims to more quickly and more easily obtain redress, resulting in more cases being brought, then, in some measure, the purpose of these amendments would have been fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of the administrative cost on Internet intermediaries, we should first bear in mind the fact that Internet intermediaries already fall within the scope of POHA today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In any event, we should remember that this Bill deals with harassment, physical and online, and the use of falsehoods to affect and damage people’s lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Apparent from the many examples I gave in my speech earlier, and certainly those cited by Members themselves, this kind of conduct has very serious consequences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: People’s lives and reputations can be easily and quickly destroyed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of this happens in an online environment and on platforms where falsehoods travel quickly and the truth is often left behind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Without redress, and the remedies which this Bill proposes, it would be next to impossible for individuals to protect themselves against this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Internet intermediaries have long been unable, or perhaps unwilling, to take proactive steps to remove such content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the issue here is not so much about cost.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is about a falsehood where it is not only the right thing to do under this Bill to get redress for the individual, but I would say, it would also be socially responsible for the Internet intermediaries to remove these falsehoods and ensure that there is proper redress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill provides legislative solutions to deal with such conduct and to provide individuals with recourse and redress in an environment where the Internet intermediaries wield such power and control over the medium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun has asked whether the new regulations will harm Singapore's pro-innovation environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ultimately, the strengthened falsehoods regime under POHA will complement the companies' interest in running a responsible and positive platform which serves to improve the quality of private discourse amongst their users and improve the quality of their experiences on the platform.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will no doubt continue to work with the Internet intermediaries to develop operationally feasible solutions that can be taken into account under the new section 16BB(3) in the Bill, which clause 20 introduces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to some questions on online harassment and the anonymity of harassers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay, in particular, raised the issue of anonymity in cyberspace, the identification of online perpetrators not being so easily done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This issue of identifying such perpetrators was also raised during the Second Reading of POHA back in 2014.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The problem of online anonymity is not unique to offences under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, it is a serious and growing problem, not just in POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Law enforcement agencies worldwide have had to face challenges in tackling cybercrimes and cyber-enabled crimes, where criminals have sought to hide behind the relative anonymity of the Internet to cause harm to society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, a person who uses a fake moniker or other means to conceal his identity, can still be identified by the investigation efforts of law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments to POHA are intended to provide tools to deal with the unique nature of online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the amendments, even if the source of the falsehood is, for example, hiding behind a virtual private network address and cannot be tracked down, is anonymous or refuses to take down the falsehood, the victim has other options aimed at stopping the falsehood, the spread of the falsehood and also making the appropriate corrections.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The victim may apply for a stop publication order to require other parties to stop publishing the false statement or substantially similar statements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, or in the alternative, he may apply for a disabling order or a targeted correction order, depending on what is the right correction to deal with and address the false statements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These latter orders can require Internet intermediaries to disable access to the falsehood or to ensure that corrections are distributed to those who access the falsehood.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked questions about challenges involved in preserving evidence, especially online ones where the content could be posted on Instagram stories, where the material is sometimes transient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Features, such as what Ms Rahayu Mahzam has mentioned, are ephemeral and cannot be viewed once a certain period of time has elapsed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, that is a challenge to preserving the evidence, but that is also not unique to POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While evidence can be obtained through the investigation efforts of law enforcement agencies, victims and applicants can obviously also take practical steps to preserve the evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to the "doxxing" provisions and, as I have heard the speeches, there has been unanimous support for these new provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members, such as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Rahayu Mahzam, Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Louis Ng, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira and Prof Lim Sun Sun have all spoken about or raised the issue of online vigilantism.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Briefly, it is information which, on its own or with other information, identifies or could be used to identify an individual.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked, in particular, as an example, if a vehicle plate number could fall under the definition of "identity information".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, as with all cases before our Courts, the judges will have to look at the specific facts and overall context of each case, to look at the circumstances in which it took place, to look at the holistic context of the facts and circumstances, and then make an overall assessment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Louis Ng as well as Mr Pritam Singh have also raised queries pertaining to the ambit of the offences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will outline the type of conduct that these offences target as well as conduct that will not breach the law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The offence of doxxing requires the ingredient of the publisher’s intention or knowledge based on the objective circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As is the case with many other intention or knowledge-based offences today, for example, even under those which you can find in sections 3 and 7 of the existing Act, the Court must look at all the facts and circumstances before it determines if there was such intention or knowledge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not looking at an overt act like stalking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, some examples are set out in the act on stalking, but it is looking at circumstances from which one infers or derives an understanding of the intention behind the act itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked about the factors which a Court might consider when deciding whether there was intention or knowledge present in a case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, and I think you have heard me say, it is fact-specific.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, you cannot quite constrain the Court to always be considering a set of facts and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But to the extent helpful and illustrative, let me set out some of these facts which could be considered in a case to determine intent or knowledge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, words or actions that accompany the publication of someone’s personal information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overt acts and declarations are essential facts from which the Court may infer an intention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if A publishes B's personal information and encourages others, along with the publication, to harass B or to find a way to incite or to use violence against B, then the Court could infer that there was the necessary intent in this case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the Court will also look at the context in which the personal information was made available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in another example, if A supplies B's personal information in an online forum, and I think this is close to some of the examples that Members have cited, that is dedicated to hunting down and committing violence against "wrongdoers", the objective circumstances would point to the inference that A knew or had reasonable cause to believe that his post would facilitate the use of unlawful violence against the victim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the act itself may be neutral but the act of putting it in a forum which is for the self-declared purposes of trying to seek online vigilantism or to incite violence, that would then be taken together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the relevant context behind the act will also be considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The provisions do not distinguish between the original publisher and someone who then reposts the publication.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Rather, the law looks at the intention of the person who publishes the personal information or the knowledge that he had when he published that information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To illustrate, the original publisher of the personal information might not have ill-intent but someone who reposts the same information may then have the malicious objective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The key factor is the intention behind the publication, whether original or the republication, and each case will have to be considered on its own facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked about a hyperlinking occasion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, I did not quite get the specific facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, please correct me if I am wrong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I understand Mr Pritam Singh's example was that if you hyperlink identity information, and in the context of the example, it was a lawyer, and the question that was posed is, "Why is a lawyer behaving in this way?" Then, on those facts, it is not a question of doxxing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will conclude my responses to the queries raised regarding the ambit of the provisions by emphasising that the nature has to be very fact-specific.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We cannot be overly prescriptive in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we could categorise and put together examples of permissible and impermissible publication of identity information, through guidelines or other informational material.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether something is or is not an offence will have to depend on the facts and, as I said, the Court has to look at each case on its own.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as I also mentioned at the outset, putting all of these together into one body and to allow a framework within which a prosecution can take place, will, in itself, over time, develop a body of jurisprudence, and the application of the provisions will be guided by the Court which looks at each case and develops the jurisprudence in common law as the cases move along.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked why POHA does not apply to the Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the case of POHA, that is the case, and the Government has taken a view that it will not avail itself of remedies under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, it will not be subject to provisions under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As to how officers of the Government can be held accountable, that can always be done in the usual forum like in Parliament, as in the usual case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh is aware of that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would just like to reiterate that as important as it is to have this piece of legislation to deal with remedies for harassment online and offline, equally important is the social consciousness and, of course, public education to shape behaviour.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have taken note of Members' suggestions which may be outside of the scope of legislation but which are nonetheless helpful as we work towards a society that, not just through legislation but as a whole, frowns on harassment and frowns on what is effectively bullying, whether online or offline.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have worked and will continue to work with the media and other stakeholders to raise general public awareness of their rights and remedies under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But before that, I would like to thank the Senior Minister of State for going through the examples that were raised and providing his clarifications for them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My query is on the definition of a false statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The example I have used, which the Senior Minister of State referred to as an opinion, went like this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: People who listen to black metal music may commit violence in the real world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I can understand that in the context of a false statement, there is the usual objective test which in law and that statement may not qualify as a false statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But in clause 3, the definition of a false statement includes a misleading statement and that complicates the situation a little bit vis-a-vis whether that is an opinion or whether that is a misleading statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If it is a misleading statement, then an individual who made that statement potentially could have action taken against him under the Bill, of course, through the civil route.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can the Senior Minister of State please clarify?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What this Bill seeks to do is to look at statements of fact which are directly and positively false.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think the Courts have clear jurisprudence on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But also indirectly through omission otherwise false or misleading in itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my earlier speech, I cited an example as to how if you omit certain key facts which are material to understanding, then the image or the view that is communicated is otherwise false because of the omission, and not so much because of a positive statement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Well, it depends on the circumstances in which he went on to identify the actual culprit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I would imagine that in such a scenario, Members would remember I spoke about there being a defence of reasonableness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if you portray someone as being the perpetrator when actually it is not, then I think I would doubt that the Court would say it is unreasonable for the person to then point in the direction of the actual perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Let the Court look at the facts of each case and understand the context and reasons behind the posting even by the second person.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Just a point of clarification for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: He mentioned about the Government being precluded from using the POHA to take action.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Just for clarity, individuals, in particular, public sector workers or civil servants, they can actually make use of POHA vis-a-vis versus perpetrators or they themselves are perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I explained that in my earlier speeches on the Member's example on workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just to follow up on that earlier example vis-a-vis the misleading statement, I understand what the Senior Minister of State has said about it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The issue is, in the context that I provided, that statement has caused damage to a certain entity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that entity seeks to prove in Court that the statement actually, in and of itself, is misleading, and because of those circumstances, loss has accrued to the band.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Would they be able to rely on POHA?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that is not to say that should you have a statement that has affected a business entity economically or that might otherwise be defamatory of an individual, those civil remedies still apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And parties can still avail themselves of that even if the statement does not fall under POHA.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.45 pm.
